name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
title: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
answer: Opposing counsel and docket patterns is the study of how lawyers and courts behave across the life of a case, using public filings to see what each side tends to file, when, and with what result. It sits inside litigation prediction and judicial analytics, where the goal is not certainty but a clearer picture of likely next steps and pressure points. In the AI context, this includes the 148 active AI lawsuits the site tracks, 92 of them intellectual property, because those dockets show how counsel frame disputes over training data, model outputs, and trade secrets. The work covers motion practice, scheduling orders, discovery disputes, and settlement signals, all tied to the specific judge and opposing firm. It is a practical lens for a litigator who wants to prepare for an adversary's habits rather than guess at them.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on docket data, court filings, and counsel records, usually pulled from public systems such as PACER and state court portals. A typical stack includes a database of docket entries, a document store for briefs and orders, and a pipeline that extracts parties, counsel, judges, and motion types. The site's 29 AI case law precedents can act as a curated reference layer for how courts have handled similar AI issues. Analysts also need judge profiles, local rules, and scheduling histories to compare one courtroom with another. Because docket feeds arrive in different formats, normalization and entity resolution are constant chores.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start by collecting every docket entry for a case and tagging each event, such as a motion to dismiss, a discovery request, or a scheduling conference. They then build features from timing, sequence, and outcome, for example how long an opposing counsel typically takes to respond or how often a judge grants a particular motion. Statistical models and, increasingly, machine learning rank likely next filings or estimate the chance of a motion succeeding. The same approach can profile an opposing firm across many cases, revealing patterns that a single docket would hide. Human review remains essential because docket text is messy and context changes the meaning of a filing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is a first concern because docket data can be incomplete, sealed, or mislabeled, and any prediction inherits those flaws. Privacy and access rules matter, especially when filings contain personal information or when a court restricts public view. Counsel analytics also carries risk of bias if historical patterns reflect systemic disparities rather than the merits of a case. Professional conduct rules in many jurisdictions require lawyers to supervise AI tools and verify outputs, and unauthorized practice of law rules limit who may give legal advice. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages offer a map of these constraints, but they are reference material, not a substitute for checking local rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: As AI litigation grows, the 148 active AI lawsuits tracked here will keep adding docket data, and the 92 intellectual property cases will likely drive much of the analysis. Expect more granular counsel-level metrics, real-time docket alerts, and models that combine judge history with opposing firm behavior. Courts are slowly opening more data through e-filing standards, which will improve coverage but also raise new privacy questions. The field is moving toward transparency about model limits, because a prediction that cannot be explained is hard to defend in a professional setting. Over time, opposing counsel and docket patterns may become a standard part of case strategy, not a specialist curiosity.
